name: r3-revise-2
statement: A loop is an absorbing hazard for the cued base. The sampler opens it only at impasse positions, and how far along a solution impasses appear depends on the sampler: under T 0.6, impasses come early enough to trap medium-length solutions the base would otherwise finish, while at T >= 1.0 (with or without tail truncation) only a fixed, problem-specific set of long solutions reaches one, and those problems are mostly lost anyway. So a sampler moves accuracy only through loops it creates on finishable problems: accuracy is flat across T >= 1 samplers while cap hits vary, cap hits at T >= 1 are nested inside the T 0.6 cap-hit set, and many T 0.6 cap-hit problems are solved at T 1.0.
scope: Olmo-3-1025-7B base with the opening cue on MATH-500 and the clean harder 328, cap 16,384, grader v3, temperatures 0.6-1.5 with or without top-p / min-p truncation. Revises r2-all-2. Its review found that top-p 0.95 at T 1.0 added cap hits and loops but cost only 1 point, not the predicted 12, and that accuracy stayed within 404-412 across four T >= 1 samplers while cap hits ranged 27-58. Here the surprise-level optimum is dropped: what matters is whether new loops land on problems the base would finish. Does not cover the plain base's drift on short problems, RL's own temperature insensitivity, or weight edits.

imports.finding: A started repetition loop survives as a product of per-step continuation probabilities; untruncated sampling never locks, while top-p locks once every loop token clears the threshold.
imports.how: Makes the loop absorbing under truncation or low temperature and escapable at T 1.0 untruncated, so the sampler sets the hazard per impasse.

imports.finding: Truncation samplers help only once temperature has collapsed accuracy; on robust models at T 0.7-1.0 their paired gain is at most about +3 points.
imports.how: Supports the flat accuracy at T >= 1 across truncation rules: the cued base at T 1.0 is in the robust regime, where truncation only shifts how already-lost long problems fail.

imports.finding: Loops arise where the progress action's probability is spread over alternatives and a cyclic action keeps its mass; harder problems loop more and low temperature picks the cycle.
imports.how: Defines the impasse positions: places where progress mass is diffuse, which accumulate with solution length, so long solutions meet one first.

explains.quote: No truncation rule beats untruncated sampling on MATH-500 at T 1.0
explains.how: At T >= 1 the new loops land on long problems that were mostly lost anyway, so accuracy does not move.

explains.quote: rule-A loops 0 -> 34 at min-p 0.1, 12 at top-p 0.95
explains.how: Truncation turns escapable impasses on long solutions into locked loops, raising loops and cap hits without changing which problems are lost.
At T 0.6 the hazard is high enough to trap medium-length solutions, so loops now take finishable problems and accuracy falls.

explains.quote: Restarting cap hits (up to 3 attempts) gives 414/500
explains.how: Most T 0.6 cap hits are finishable problems, so fresh attempts recover about half of them.
T 1.0 cap hits are the impasse set itself (long, mostly unsolvable for the base), so restarts there recover little, unlike at T 0.6.
Removing top-p at T 0.6 lowers the hazard only slightly, so loops still take medium-length problems.

explains.quote: they are the long problems for both
explains.how: The base's T 1.0 cap hits sit on the problems with long solutions, the fixed impasse set.

explains.quote: 140 base first answers exceed 12,000 tokens (11 right)
explains.how: Long base answers at T 1.0 are almost all lost, so converting them into loops costs almost nothing.
Length marks the impasse set: the longer the base's answer, the more likely it is lost.
Short solutions never reach an impasse, so they are nearly always right whatever the sampler.
On the 328, T 0.6 traps many finishable problems. T 1.0 releases them, and the remaining 77 cap hits are the long impasse problems.

explains.quote: of 123 problems RL right and cued base wrong at T 0.6, 85 were cap hits
explains.how: At T 0.6 most of the gap to RL is loops on problems RL finishes, the finishable problems the hazard traps.
A prefix that already holds an impasse-bearing solution keeps the hazard high, so continuations loop again.

conflicts.quote: RL-prefix minus own-prefix finish rate +32.1 points [17.9, 46.2]
conflicts.how: From RL's prefix the same problems finish far more often, so impasses depend on the path taken, not only on the problem. The 'fixed per-problem impasse set' is a simplification.
Some T 1.0 cap hits are unfinished drift, not loops. The theory treats them as the same impasse set without separate evidence.

conflicts.quote: T 1.5 + min-p 0.1 removes them (0 loops, 29 cap)
conflicts.how: At T 1.5 cap hits stay near 29 with no loops, so the impasse set fails by drift there. The theory explains why accuracy stays flat, but not why loops disappear entirely.

rival: Loops land on the problems the base cannot solve (hardness-only reading of 2512.12895). Under it, T 0.6 cap-hit problems are mostly ones the base also gets wrong at T 1.0, and the T 0.6 penalty comes from something else (sharper slips). Separation: the share of T 0.6 cap-hit problems that the T 1.0 cued base gets right. The rival predicts about a third. This theory predicts about 60 %, together with T 1.0 cap hits nested inside the T 0.6 set.

predictions.experiment: Base + opening cue, the clean harder 328, T 1.0 / top-p 1.0 / min-p 0.1, cap 16,384, one sample, grader v3: number right (min-p 0 gives 164 with 77 cap hits)
predictions.refuted_by: 150 or fewer right (truncation-made loops take finishable hard problems) or 176 or more

predictions.experiment: Same run (base + cue, hard 328, T 1.0 / min-p 0.1): cap hits
predictions.refuted_by: 82 or fewer cap hits (truncation does not lock impasses on hard problems)

predictions.experiment: Base + opening cue, MATH-500 n=500, T 0.8 / top-p 1.0, cap 16,384, one sample, grader v3: number right (T 0.6 / top-p 1.0 gives 378, T 1.0 gives 410)
predictions.refuted_by: 390 or fewer right (the T 0.8 loss is linear in temperature, not limited to loops on finishable problems)

predictions.experiment: Offline: share of the cued base's T 0.6 / top-p 1.0 cap-hit problems that the cued base solves at T 1.0 (MATH-500).
predictions.recipe: Files: iterate-runs:abaybektursun-1114-151718-d4fa/answers.jsonl (base, cue, T 0.6 / top-p 1.0, MATH-500) and studies/rlneurons/results/rln4/t1_t2_items-01/per_problem.json. Take one row per problem_index from d4fa (first in file order). Set C = problem_index values whose d4fa row has cap_hit true. Statistic: number of problems in C with t1_right true in per_problem.json, divided by |C|. A missing per_problem entry counts as not right.
predictions.refuted_by: fraction below 0.45 (T 0.6 loops land mainly on problems the base cannot solve)

predictions.experiment: Offline: nesting of the T 1.0 cap-hit set inside the T 0.6 cap-hit set (cued base, MATH-500).
predictions.recipe: Files: studies/rlneurons/results/rln4/t1_t2_items-01/per_problem.json and iterate-runs:abaybektursun-1114-151718-d4fa/answers.jsonl. Set A = problem_index values with t1_cap_hit true in per_problem.json (27 expected). Set C = d4fa cap_hit true (one row per problem_index, first in file order). Statistic: |A intersect C| / |A|.
predictions.refuted_by: fraction below 0.5 (T 1.0 cap hits are not a subset of the T 0.6 impasse set)

predictions.experiment: Offline: the same nesting on the clean harder 328.
predictions.recipe: Files: iterate-runs:abaybektursun-1114-151534-e72c/answers.jsonl (base, cue, T 1.0, clean 328) and s3://pg-lineage-769063704696/results/rlneurons/r3/base-01/out/F_hard.jsonl (base, cue, T 0.6 / top-p 0.95, harder set n = 400), restricted to the 328 problems flagged none in results/rln3/rln3_overlap.json, matched on unique_id.
